issues.explanation: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events are not well linked to the stated trauma of witnessing childhood domestic violence, especially when the other trigger items center on male presence and shouting. This trigger is not impossible, but in this profile it stands out as insufficiently connected to the rest of the formulation.

Listening for signs that someone is entering the home suggests a burglary/home-intrusion threat theme, which is weakly connected to the selected trauma-specific cues and memory/appraisal content centered on domestic violence. It pulls the threat profile toward external break-in danger rather than reenacted interpersonal violence.

Noticing weapons or dangerous objects in any environment implies a generalized weapon-attack threat theme, but the trauma type and the rest of the items do not support a weapon-focused formulation. This makes the threat node less coherent with the memory and appraisal content.

'I have failed in my most important role in life' is a broad role-failure appraisal that is not clearly anchored to the selected trauma memories or other appraisals. The other negative appraisals emphasize weakness and disconnection; this item introduces a different theme without enough support elsewhere in the profile.

Drug use is not well supported by the rest of the five-component profile. The strongest formulation link is Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies, and the other strategies clearly fit trigger-driven internal threat management, whereas drug use introduces a more severe coping pattern without corresponding support from the other selected items.

vignette:
Carlos was six years old, crouched at the top of the stairs in his family's small apartment in San Juan, when his father's fist connected with his mother's jaw. He can still see it, not as a story that unfolded, but as a single frozen image: the way her head snapped to the side, the arc of a gold earring flying loose and skittering across the linoleum. That moment exists in his mind as a vivid, snapshot picture, crystalline and unchanging, and whenever it surfaces he is flooded with a guilt so complete it feels physical-the belief that he should have done something, that he was a coward for staying hidden. Now sixty-four, a divorced jeweler working alone at his bench in a small shop in Chicago, Carlos has spent decades trying not to think about that night. He suppresses the memory deliberately, pushing it down the moment it threatens to surface, and he constantly monitors his own thoughts for any sign that he is losing control. He has come to believe that if he lets his mind relax, even for a moment, something dangerous will break loose inside him.

The trouble is that his daily life is full of triggers. Shouting, even playful shouting from a customer across the street, makes his chest tighten. Male presence is the worst-when a man he doesn't know well enters his shop, Carlos finds himself watching the man's hands, scanning for potential weapons, unable to focus on anything else. Confrontations, even minor disagreements over a repair price, send him into a state of hypervigilance that lasts for hours. He has come to believe that he is a weak person, fundamentally broken, because he cannot handle what other people handle every day. These appraisals feed back into his threat monitoring: because he believes he is weak, he scans every environment more intensely, certain that he will be caught off guard. And the more he watches, the more he notices-a customer's bulky jacket, a tool left on the counter-which confirms his sense that danger is everywhere. Even when his daughter tells him he is safe, he finds it impossible to believe her.

The causal loops have tightened over the years. Each time a male customer raises his voice, Carlos's memory of his mother's face flashes vividly before him, and the guilt resurfaces. That guilt reinforces his belief that he failed in his most important role-first as a son who didn't protect his mother, then as a husband who couldn't keep his marriage together. He has lost his connection to his community and culture; he no longer attends the annual Puerto Rican festival in Humboldt Park, because the crowds and the noise feel too dangerous. His avoidance of relaxation means he works through his lunch breaks, hunched over a loupe, and his constant thought-monitoring exhausts him. The more he suppresses the memory, the more intrusively it returns, and the more he feels he is going crazy. He has begun to notice that he startles when a customer simply clears his throat, and he has started keeping his workshop door locked, only opening it for women or for men he knows well.

What finally brought Carlos to seek help was a moment three weeks ago. A man in his fifties, roughly his father's age at the time of the violence, came in to have a watch band adjusted. The man was polite, soft-spoken, but when he leaned over the counter, his shadow fell across Carlos in a particular way, and Carlos froze-unable to speak, unable to move, the snapshot of his mother's earring spinning across the floor filling his vision. The customer left without his watch. Carlos sat at his bench for an hour afterward, monitoring his thoughts, telling himself he was weak, that he had failed again. He is terrified that he is losing his mind, but what he hopes for, barely daring to name it, is that someone might finally tell him how to stop watching for the blow that never comes.
